# KaidoPlan — a project planner for AI coding teams

> KaidoPlan is a desktop app that keeps the WBS, dependencies and dates of an AI-assisted project in one local `.kaido` plan file, computes the critical path, and flags scheduling violations before they cost a delivery date. This file records only facts that can be checked in the app, its public repository and the pages linked below. Independent software by cygnus, not a company.

Last updated 2026-11-16. Current public release: v3.11.5 (2026-11-16). No claims are made for features that have not shipped.

## What it is

- **Problem**: AI agents (Claude Code, Codex and similar) execute tasks one at a time, so the plan itself ends up scattered across chat history. Task lists look finished while the deadline still moves.
- **Product**: a planning workbench that holds structure, dependencies, dates and progress in one plan that both people and agents can inspect.
- **Platform**: macOS 14 or later, Apple silicon and Intel (universal build).
- **Plan file**: a single local plain-JSON file with the `.kaido` extension, `formatVersion` 2. It can be read, edited, diffed and validated outside the app.

## What it computes

- **Forward and backward scheduling** over dependencies and constraints produces the **critical path**, per-task slack, and the resulting finish date.
- **Violations** are surfaced rather than hidden: date conflicts, dependency cycles, and tasks scheduled outside the project window.
- **WBS import**: a task breakdown can be imported and turned into a dependency graph instead of being retyped.
- **Agent interface**: a built-in MCP server (stdio JSON-RPC, **21 tools**) and a CLI cover tasks, dependencies, resources, baselines, scheduling, violation checks and WBS import.

## Pricing (direct download)

- **30-day full-feature trial**: every feature unlocked, no account, no card.
- **KaidoPlan Pro — USD 9.99 per year**: a subscription gives continued access to all features after the trial, including AI write-back (task status, actual dates, new tasks) through the MCP/CLI tools and unlimited delivery-report exports. Cancel anytime.
- **When the trial ends the app does not stop**: it drops to the free tier — the whole planning workbench, AI read-only over the MCP/CLI tools, and three delivery-report exports a month. Only AI write-back and unlimited exports need Pro. Plans are never locked and never leave the machine.
- Direct-download purchases carry a **14-day no-questions-asked refund**.
- Checkout is processed by Paddle.com Market Ltd as Merchant of Record.
- Eligible Mac App Store users can start a one-month trial through the in-app subscription.

project planner · AI coding teams

# AI says done.
Deadline moved.

Claude Code, Codex and other agents work task by task. KaidoPlan is a macOS app that holds the WBS, dependencies and dates in one local plan, and computes the one chain that decides when you actually deliver.

Download KaidoPlan for macOSSee a plan check

macOS 14+ · 30-day full-feature trial, no account · Local .kaido files

The macOS plan workbench
Critical path · The chain that sets your end dateViolations · Conflicting dates, cycles, out-of-range tasksLocal first · Project data stays on your device
Why another task list

## Task management is solved.
Knowing what still lands is not.

Every AI project management tool already gives you somewhere to keep tasks. What none of them compute is which dependency chain sets your end date — or that a two-day slip upstream just ate your review window. KaidoPlan does the arithmetic a checklist does not.

01 / DECOMPOSE

### Break the work into a WBS

Tasks, groups and milestones, each with an effort estimate. An agent imports and updates the plan over MCP or the CLI.

02 / SCHEDULE

### Compute the critical path

Dependencies, constraints and a work calendar produce real dates. The critical path tells you the earliest the project can finish — and which tasks still have slack.

03 / CHECK

### Catch conflicts while they are cheap

Cycles, dates outside the project window, deadline conflicts and blocked chains turn red in the workbench. Before the slip reaches your client, not after.

A 30-second check

## Every task says done.
Two dates no longer agree.

An agent reports progress. It rarely reports that the plan stopped adding up. Run the check and the arithmetic comes back in red.

API designends 11-01doneServer implementationends 11-06doneClient integrationstarts 11-04 · predecessor ends 11-07date conflictJoint acceptancecritical path · 0 days slackblocks the end date

Nothing here is an error in the code the agent wrote. It is an error in the schedule — and it is the kind no chat transcript will tell you about. Example plan. Screens are from the macOS app.

A clear division of work

## People set the bounds. AI executes.
The plan stays checkable.

01 · Define

Set the goal, dates and acceptance criteria.

02 · Plan

Have AI break down the WBS, connect dependencies and calculate a schedule.

03 · Review

Inspect progress, conflicts and the critical path in the Gantt chart.

04 · Execute

AI implements tasks and writes back status as the plan evolves.

What happens after the trial?

An active subscription is required for continued access to all features. Your `.kaido` project files stay on your device.

I bought it on the App Store. Does this license work?

The two subscriptions are purchased separately. The App Store subscription unlocks Pro in the App Store build, and the license sold here unlocks Pro in the direct download. If you bought one and need the other, email me — I'll move you over instead of charging you twice.

What if I don't like it?

Refund within 14 days, no questions and no exit survey. The refund policy is one page because it only has one rule.

Ship notes, once every week or two

New versions and what changed, one concrete AI workflow, and known issues with fix dates. No promo blasts, no countdowns, unsubscribe in one click.

# AI 说做完了，
交付日还是滑了。

Claude Code、Codex 以及其它智能体一项一项往下干。KaidoPlan 是一款 macOS 应用，把 WBS、依赖和日期放进一份本地计划，算出真正决定你什么时候能交付的那条链。

下载 KaidoPlan for macOS看一次计划校验

macOS 14+ · 30 天全功能试用，不需要账号 · 本地 .kaido 文件

macOS 计划工作台
关键路径 · 决定交付日期的那条链计划校验 · 日期冲突、循环依赖、超期任务本地优先 · 不上传项目数据
为什么不是又一个待办清单

## 管任务这件事已经解决了。
知道工期还落不落地，没有。

现在每个 AI 项目管理工具都已经给了你一个放任务的地方。但没有一个会算：哪条依赖链决定了你的交付日期，或者上游滑了两天、正好吃掉你的评审窗口。这份算术，待办清单不做。

01 / 拆解

### 把工作拆成 WBS

任务、分组和里程碑，每一项都带工时估算。AI 可以通过 MCP 或 CLI 导入并更新这份计划。

02 / 排期

### 算出关键路径

依赖、时限和工作日历推算出真实日期。关键路径告诉你项目最早什么时候能完成——以及哪些任务还有余量。

03 / 校验

### 在冲突还便宜的时候发现它

循环依赖、超出项目窗口的日期、截止日期冲突、被卡住的关键任务，在工作台里变红。赶在滑期传到客户那里之前，而不是之后。

30 秒校验

## 任务全都标了完成，
两个日期对不上了。

智能体会报进度，但它几乎不会报「这份计划已经加不起来了」。跑一次校验，算术结果会用红字回来。

接口设计11-01 结束完成服务端实现11-06 结束完成客户端联调11-04 开工 · 前驱 11-07 才结束日期冲突联合验收关键路径 · 余量 0 天压住交付日

这里没有一处是 AI 写错的代码，全都是排期对不上——而这一种错，任何一份聊天记录都不会告诉你。示例计划。界面截自 macOS 应用。

A clear division of work

Guides

# Guides, answers and comparisons

Everything here assumes the same starting point: an AI agent is writing code task by task, and you still have to say when the project ships.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## Start here

Install, plan and check a real project.

- Set up a KaidoPlan plan in ten minutesMost planning failures are not tool failures.

- A delivery check you can run in five minutesAn agent that reports progress honestly can still leave you with a plan that no longer adds up.

## Use cases

When a plan earns its keep, and when it does not.

- Where a plan earns its keepThree situations where a task list is not enough: one developer with several agents, parallel sessions on one plan, and a date you have to defend. Includes the cases where this is the wrong tool.

## Questions

The specific things people search for before they try a planning tool.

- How do I keep a project plan in sync across Claude Code sessions?Short answer: stop keeping the plan in the conversation.

- The agent marked every task done — why did the deadline still slip?Because <em>done</em> is a property of a task, and the delivery date is a property of a graph.

- What is a critical path, and why does an AI project need one?The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in the plan.

- How do I calculate a critical path on a Mac?Three options on macOS, and where each one breaks.

- How do I break an AI coding project into a WBS?Break it down by what can be verified independently, not by what feels like a phase.

- How do I track dependencies between tasks an agent executes?Record them as data, not as instructions in a prompt.

- Is there an MCP server for a project plan?Yes — KaidoPlan has one built in.

- Why do AI-assisted projects still miss deadlines?Because writing code faster does not shorten the chain that decides the end date — and it makes the plan look healthy while that chain stays exactly as long as it was.

- How do I export a delivery report for a client?A delivery report is not a screenshot of a task list.

## Compare

What KaidoPlan does that the obvious alternative does not — and where the alternative wins.

- KaidoPlan vs a HANDOFF.md fileA handoff file is the cheapest coordination mechanism that works.

- KaidoPlan vs Linear or Todoist over MCPBoth let an agent create tasks.

- KaidoPlan vs a spreadsheet GanttThe spreadsheet was never the problem.

## What the agent can do

The 21 MCP tools and the CLI, grouped by what you would actually ask for.

- The plan is a file, not an accountThree tools, one object: a <code>.

- Tasks and the WBSSix tools that cover the structure: create, read, filter, change, delete, and bulk import a breakdown you already have.

- Scheduling and the critical pathTwo tools turn a dependency graph into an answer: when does this finish, and which tasks decide that.

- Violation checksThe plan admits what is broken, on demand, in a list you can act on.

- Status write-backThe difference between an agent that reports progress and one that records it: a completion time that a conflict check can use.

- ResourcesA plan that says <em>three days</em> is making an assumption about who is doing the work.

- Baselines and varianceWithout a frozen schedule, <em>it slipped</em> is an opinion.

- The command lineEverything the app can do to the plan, from a terminal — which is also the shortest path to putting a schedule check in CI.

- Connecting an agentFive clients, one switch each.

One entry per public version, with a permanent page for each.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/use-cases.html

Use cases

# Where a plan earns its keep

A task list is enough until a date matters. These are the three situations where the gap between "every task is done" and "the date still holds" decides whether the project ships.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## 01 — One developer, several agents, one delivery date

You are building a three-week deliverable on your own, and the work is spread across Claude Code, Codex or whichever agent you have open. Every session reports progress. The task list gets greener each day. Then someone asks when it ships, and you open the list and realise the client integration sits behind an API task that quietly grew two subtasks on Tuesday.

Nothing in that story is a coding error. Each task was genuinely finished or genuinely in progress. What went uncalculated is the one thing an agent never reports: which chain of dependencies is setting the end date.

This is the case the app is built for. The work is broken into a WBS, dependencies are connected, and forward and backward scheduling produce a real finish date plus per-task slack. The chain with zero slack is usually two or three tasks, and it is rarely the ones that dominate a status update.

What changes: the delivery date stops being a number someone typed into a cell and becomes a consequence of the graph. When the graph changes — including when an agent changes it — the date moves with it.

## 02 — Parallel agent sessions editing the same plan

Several sessions run on the same project. Each one only knows its own context window. The plan ends up scattered across transcripts: one session moved a date, another added a task, a third closed something that the first is still waiting on. Nobody can say which version is current, and no agent can see the whole shape.

Keeping the plan in one local `.kaido` file gives every session the same object to read and write. A built-in MCP server and a CLI cover tasks, dependencies, resources, baselines, scheduling, violation checks and WBS import, so an agent reads the plan before it acts instead of guessing from chat history.

The plan is also checkable, which matters more than it sounds. Violation checks surface date conflicts, dependency cycles and tasks scheduled outside the project window. A cycle is what two agents create when each waits for the other, and it is the failure mode that a chat transcript will never show you.

What changes: parallel work stops producing parallel versions of the plan.

## 03 — A date you have to defend to someone else

You owe a date to a client, a partner or a manager. Quote it early and you cannot deliver; quote it late and you lose the work. What you need at that moment is not optimism but an argument: this date is set by these three tasks, everything else has slack, and here is what breaks it.

The critical path gives you that argument, because it is computed rather than asserted. A task with zero slack blocks the end date; a task with four days of slack can absorb a slip without moving it. That distinction is invisible in a list where every row says done.

Delivery reports can be exported for the person who asked. They show the plan, the computed dates and the outstanding violations at the time of export.

What changes: the date comes with its own reasoning, so the conversation is about the graph instead of about whether you are being pessimistic.

## When this is not the tool

Being specific about the edges is cheaper than a refund.

- Not a collaboration platform. There is no cloud sync and no real-time multi-user editing. The plan is a file; sharing it across people means sending the file. Teams that need a shared live board should look elsewhere.

- Not a kanban replacement. If you only need to see what is in progress and who owns it, a board does that with less setup. This app is about dates and dependencies, and it assumes you care about them.

- macOS only. macOS 14 or later, Apple silicon and Intel. There is no Windows or Linux build.

- It does not estimate for you. Effort and durations are your assertions. The scheduler does arithmetic on what you claim; it does not know that your last three integrations took four days each instead of two.

- No telemetry. Nothing is sent about how you use the app. The trade-off is that usage analytics inside the product do not exist — what you cannot measure, you have to ask about.

## How to tell if you are in one of these

Three questions. If one of them is a yes, the arithmetic is worth running:

- Does this project have a date that someone outside the work is waiting on?

- Do at least two tasks have to happen in a fixed order?

- Is more than one person — or more than one agent session — changing the plan?

If all three are no, you have a to-do list and you should keep it. If two or more are yes, the failure you are heading for is the one this page opened with: every task done, the date gone.

KaidoPlan runs on macOS 14 or later.

Changelog

# Release notes

One entry per public release, newest first. Each version keeps a permanent URL, and the same entries are available as RSS.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## v3.4.0 — 2026-11-07

One switch per MCP client, a stdio mode, and a stable port.

- Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and WorkBuddy each get one switch. Flipping it writes only the `mcpServers.kaidoplan` key into that client's configuration — indentation, key order and line endings elsewhere are preserved byte for byte. Turning it off removes the same key.

- Each row reports its own state: connected, configuration needs updating, write failure with a reason and retry, not connected, client not installed. One client failing does not affect the others.

- The app binary can act as a stdio MCP server with `--mcp-stdio`: no window, no Dock icon, and no separate CLI install required for a client to start it.

- The MCP service is on by default on the loopback address; a previously stored explicit off setting is respected rather than overwritten.

- The bound port is persisted across launches, with a fallback range of 56 private ports when it is taken. A fallback does not overwrite the stored preference.

- When the endpoint or token changes, configurations of enabled clients are rewritten automatically.

Permanent page for v3.4.0

Earlier versions are listed in GitHub Releases. The version on this page is the public release; development builds are not announced here.

## Questions this page does not answer

How do I get notified?

The RSS feed at /changelog.xml, or the release watch on GitHub. There is no mailing list for releases.

Is the App Store build the same version?

The direct download is what this page tracks. Store versions follow their own review schedule.

简体中文

# KaidoPlan Privacy Policy

Last updated: 15 November 2026

KaidoPlan ("the app") does not collect your personal data and does not send anything anywhere
in the background. The only outbound transfer is feedback you submit yourself: nothing is sent
until you write something under Help ▸ Report a Problem… and press Submit, and what you chose to
send becomes publicly visible in an issue in the public repository.

- No data collection: no accounts, no analytics, no background crash reporting,
no advertising, no third-party SDKs. The app never uploads anything on its own.

- Feedback you submit (the only outbound transfer): sent only when you press
Submit in the Help ▸ Report a Problem… panel; until then what you typed stays on your Mac.
What is sent: your description, machine details (version, build number, distribution channel,
macOS version, Mac model identifier, UI language, license type), and — only if you
tick the box for them — logs and crash reports, redacted before packaging (paths keep
only their last two components). The feedback is posted to this project's
public issue tracker, where anyone
can read and search it and where it may be indexed by search engines and third-party archives;
submitting with your own GitHub account shows that account name, while having the maintainer's
account (GitHub `cygnusyang`) post it for you does not show your account details
(the body is exactly what you wrote). You cannot delete it yourself — to have
it removed, leave a comment on the original issue. Never uploaded: the
contents of your `.kaido` project files, project file paths, recent project
bookmarks, the contents of your license file, and your email address.

- Project data stays local: the `.kaido` files you open and save
live only where you put them. The app never uploads, backs up or syncs project content.

- Recent projects: to reopen your last project on launch, the app creates a
security-scoped bookmark for files or folders you explicitly chose, and keeps it in local
preferences. Clearing "Recent projects" or removing an authorized folder deletes it.

- MCP service (off by default): when you enable it under Project ▸ MCP Service…,
the app listens on `127.0.0.1` so a locally running AI client can read and write
the same plan.

- loopback only — never the LAN, never the internet;

- every request must carry a bearer token generated locally and shown in that panel;

- only folders you authorized in that panel are reachable; anything else is refused;

- turning the switch off or resetting the token cuts access immediately.

- No third-party sharing: apart from feedback you submit yourself, which GitHub
hosts as a public issue, the app shares nothing with any third party — there is no other data
to share.

Questions: open an issue at
github.com/cygnusyang/KaidoPlan.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/guides/kaidoplan-quickstart.html

Guide · 10 minutes

# Set up a KaidoPlan plan in ten minutes

Most planning failures are not tool failures. They start with a plan that has no end date, no dependencies and no way to tell whether the arithmetic still holds. This is the shortest path to a plan that does.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## Before you start

You need macOS 14 or later and about ten minutes. No account is involved: the app never asks you to sign in, and the plan is a file on your disk. The direct download includes a 30-day trial of every feature.

`brew install --cask cygnusyang/kaidoplan/kaidoplan
brew install cygnusyang/kaidoplan/kaidoplan-cli`

The CLI is optional for planning in the GUI, but you will want it for the checks below and for anything an agent does on your behalf. If you would rather not use Homebrew, the same builds are on GitHub Releases.

## 1. Give the project a window before you add any work

Create a project and set a start and an end date. This is not decoration: the window is what every violation check is measured against. A task that finishes after the project end is a violation, and it cannot be reported if the project has no end.

The plan is stored as a single `.kaido` file — plain JSON, `formatVersion` 2. You can put it in the repository next to the code, diff it in a pull request, or read it with `jq`. It is not a database and it is not synced anywhere.

## 2. Add the work as a WBS, not as a list

Tasks, groups and milestones, each with an effort estimate. The distinction that matters: a list records what exists, a WBS records what depends on what. If two tasks can run in parallel, say so; if they cannot, the dependency is the only thing that will stop the schedule from quietly compressing into a fiction.

If you already have the breakdown in another tool, import it instead of retyping it. `wbs_import` takes a nested task tree and turns it into the plan.

## 3. Connect the dependencies

A finish-to-start dependency with an optional lag covers most real projects. Constraints — start no earlier than, finish no later than — cover the rest: a review that cannot begin before a date, a demo that cannot slip past one.

When you are done, every task should have exactly one honest answer to "what has to finish before this starts". Tasks with no predecessor are the start of a chain, and chains are what the next step computes.

## 4. Run the check before you trust the dates

`kaidoplan schedule compute --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan schedule path --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan violations --file plan.kaido`

The first command propagates dependencies and returns each task's earliest and latest dates. The second returns the critical path: the chain whose total slack is zero, which is the only chain that decides your delivery date. The third lists violations — dependency cycles, deadline conflicts, and tasks scheduled outside the project window.

Run all three after any change that touches dates. The result you are looking for is boring: no violations, and a critical path you can name out loud.

## 5. Connect the agent that will actually write the code

In the app, open the MCP service panel. Each supported client — Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and WorkBuddy — has one switch. Flipping it writes only the `mcpServers.kaidoplan` key into that client's configuration and leaves the rest of the file byte-identical, so your existing MCP servers and formatting survive. Turning it off removes the same key.

The service listens on the loopback address only, and every request has to carry the token shown in that panel. Only folders you authorized there are reachable.

During the trial, an agent can read the plan and use write tools to update task status and actual dates or add tasks. A subscription keeps AI write-back available after the trial.

## 6. What "set up" actually means

- The project has a start and an end date, and both are real.

- Every task has an owner-by-intent, an effort estimate and its predecessors.

- `violations` returns nothing.

- You can name the critical path without opening the app.

- One agent is connected, and you know whether it can write.

That is the whole setup. It is deliberately smaller than a project management methodology, because the failure mode it addresses is narrow: an agent reports every task done, and the date moved anyway.

## Questions this page does not answer

What does the free trial include?

The trial includes the planning workbench, AI read and write access, and unlimited delivery-report exports. KaidoPlan Pro is $9.99 per year for continued access to all features.

Where does the plan live?

Wherever you save the .kaido file. There is no account, no sync and no server copy; the app's only unprompted network call is the update check.

Can I keep using my current task tracker?

Yes, as long as you accept that the tracker will not tell you which chain sets the end date. KaidoPlan is the schedule layer, not a second inbox.

KaidoPlan runs on macOS 14 or later.

Try every feature free for 30 days with the direct download. Continue with full access for $9.99 per year.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/guides/delivery-check.html

Guide · reproducible

# A delivery check you can run in five minutes

An agent that reports progress honestly can still leave you with a plan that no longer adds up. The check below does not ask anyone how it is going. It asks the plan.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## Why a status report is not a delivery check

A status report answers "what is done". A delivery check answers "when does this finish, and what would have to be true for that to change". The two diverge exactly when it matters: every task says complete, and the end date has still moved, because something that was supposed to finish first finished late, or a dependency was never written down, or a task was scheduled before its predecessor ended.

None of those are coding errors. They are arithmetic errors in the plan, and they are invisible in a chat transcript. So the check runs on the file, not on the narrative.

## The four checks

### 1. Does the schedule compute at all?

`kaidoplan schedule compute --file plan.kaido`

This propagates the dependencies and returns each task's earliest and latest dates. If a dependency cycle exists, the schedule cannot be computed — which is the most useful possible failure, because it means the plan describes work that can never start.

### 2. Which chain sets the end date?

`kaidoplan schedule path --file plan.kaido`

Critical path and slack. Zero-slack tasks decide the delivery date; everything else has room. This is the answer to "what should I worry about", and it usually contains two or three tasks, not fifteen.

### 3. What does the plan admit is broken?

`kaidoplan violations --file plan.kaido`

Four classes come back, and each has exactly one correct response:

Violation

What it means

What to do

Dependency cycle

The plan says A waits for B and B waits for A

Break the cycle. Nothing downstream of it is real.

Deadline conflict

A task finishes after a constraint or the project end

Move the date, cut the scope, or move the constraint — decide deliberately.

Task outside the project window

A task starts before the project starts or ends after it ends

Either the window is wrong or the task does not belong in this project.

Blocked chain

Work that cannot proceed because an upstream item is stuck

This is the chain to escalate today, not the loudest task in the list.

### 4. Did the agent's write-back land?

`kaidoplan status batch --file plan.kaido --json`

Bulk status writes return per-entry success and failure. A failing entry does not stop the rest, which is the right behaviour and also the reason you have to read the output: partial success looks like success from a distance.

## Reading the result honestly

Three outcomes, three different conversations:

- No violations and a named critical path. The plan is internally consistent. Whether it is achievable is a different question, and the answer is not in the file.

- Violations that were already there last week. Nothing has changed, which means the check has become ritual. Fix one, then re-run.

- Violations appeared after a write-back. An agent updated status without updating dates. This is the common case, and the reason status write-back and date review belong in the same loop.

The one-sentence version

Run the check whenever an agent changes the plan, and treat a violation the same way you treat a failing test: not as bad news, but as information that arrived early enough to be useful.

## Doing it on a real repository

The plan is a file in your repo, so the check can be part of the pull request you were going to open anyway: run `violations`, paste the output, and if it is non-empty the change is not ready. That is the entire integration — no dashboard, no webhook, no account.

If you want the same four checks without a terminal, the app's workbench shows violations inline and the critical path highlighted in the Gantt chart. Same numbers, different surface.

You can also install a ready-made skill from SkillHub and run the same checks:

`skillhub install kaidoplan-delivery-check`

## Questions this page does not answer

How is this different from a burndown chart?

A burndown chart plots completed work against time. It cannot see that a dependency was never recorded, or that a completed task finished after the task that depended on it. The four checks read the dependency graph, not the totals.

Can I run the check during the free trial?

Yes. During the trial you can compute the schedule, inspect the critical path and list violations.

KaidoPlan runs on macOS 14 or later.

Try every feature free for 30 days with the direct download. Continue with full access for $9.99 per year.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/changelog/v3-4-0.html

Release · v3.4.0

# v3.4.0 — 2026-11-07

Connecting an agent stopped being a copy-and-paste exercise, and the app became its own MCP server.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

This is the permanent page for v3.4.0. It is also the current public release.

## Added

- One switch per MCP client. Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and WorkBuddy. The writer is text-level and preserving: it adds or removes only `mcpServers.kaidoplan` (Codex uses `[mcp_servers.kaidoplan]`) and leaves the rest of the file untouched, including CRLF line endings.

- Visible per-client state. Connected, configuration needs updating (the endpoint or token in the config no longer matches), write failed with a reason and a retry, not connected, client not installed.

- `--mcp-stdio` mode. The app's own executable can be launched by a client as a stdio MCP server. The mode is intercepted early in launch, so no window appears and no Dock icon is added.

## Changed

- MCP service on by default. The default flipped from off to on; an existing installation that had explicitly turned it off stays off, because only the default changed.

- Port persistence. The first successful bind is stored and preferred on restart, falling back through 56 private ports when it is taken. The stored preference is not overwritten by a fallback.

- Panel redesign. The old "copy this JSON yourself" block became the per-client switch list. A copy-configuration button remains as the manual path.

## Notes

The service listens on the loopback address only, requires the token shown in the panel, and can reach only folders authorized there. Write tools remain gated by the Pro licence after the 30-day trial; a refusal happens before anything is written to disk.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/compare/kaidoplan-vs-handoff-md.html

Comparison

# KaidoPlan vs a HANDOFF.md file

A handoff file is the cheapest coordination mechanism that works. It is also the reason nobody notices the schedule has stopped adding up.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## What a handoff file does well

A `HANDOFF.md` — or `CLAUDE.md`, or an `AGENTS.md` — is a plain file in the repository that tells the next session what is going on: what was finished, what is next, which decisions are settled. It costs nothing, it diffs, it survives tool changes, and every agent can read it. If the only problem you have is "the agent forgot what we did yesterday", a handoff file solves it and nothing else is needed.

## What it cannot do

HANDOFF.md

KaidoPlan

Shape

Prose, written by whoever updated it last

Structured plan: tasks, groups, milestones, effort, dependencies

Dates

Whatever the text says

Computed from dependencies, constraints and a project window

Critical path

Not representable

Computed, with per-task slack

Consistency

Contradictions are prose contradictions — nobody diffs them

Violations are listed: cycles, deadline conflicts, out-of-window tasks

History

Git history of a narrative

Baselines: immutable schedule snapshots you can compare actuals against

Cost

Free, zero setup

A macOS app, a file format, and ten minutes of setup

The failure is structural rather than a matter of discipline. Prose has no edges, so nothing prevents a handoff file from saying "client integration starts 11-04" in one paragraph and "server implementation ends 11-06" in another. Both sentences are true to their author, and the plan they describe cannot happen. A graph makes that contradiction a violation you can list.

## The overlap people miss

A handoff file is good at intent, and a plan is good at arithmetic. The mistake is asking one to do the other: a plan file full of design rationale is as unreadable as a WBS written in paragraphs. Keep the reasoning in `HANDOFF.md`, keep the dates and dependencies in the plan, and let the agent read both. KaidoPlan's plan is plain JSON, so an agent that can read a markdown file can read this one too — 21 MCP tools cover reading and writing it, and the CLI does the same from a shell.

## When the handoff file wins

- One person, one week, no external deadline. There is nothing to compute.

- The work is genuinely exploratory: you do not know the tasks yet, so a WBS would be fiction with dates attached.

- You are on Linux or Windows, where KaidoPlan does not run.

If two of those three are false, the handoff file is carrying a schedule it cannot represent — and the first time you need to answer "can we still ship on the 21st" it will answer with a paragraph instead of a number.

## Questions this page does not answer

Can the agent update both?

Yes. The plan is a local JSON file with a documented schema and an MCP surface; the handoff file is markdown. An agent can be told to keep dates in the plan and reasoning in the handoff file, which is usually the cleanest split.

Is a plan file still readable in a pull request?

It diffs as JSON. A date change is a one-line diff, which is more reviewable than the same change described in a paragraph.

KaidoPlan runs on macOS 14 or later.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/compare/kaidoplan-vs-linear-todoist-mcp.html

Comparison

# KaidoPlan vs Linear or Todoist over MCP

Both let an agent create tasks. Only one of them can tell you whether the project still ends on the day you promised.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## What a tracker with MCP gets right

Linear, Todoist and their peers solved capture and coordination years ago: fast entry, assignments, states, comments, notifications, mobile clients, and now an MCP server so an agent can file and update issues without a human copying text between windows. If your problem is "the agent's work never reaches the team's system of record", a tracker with MCP is the correct answer and KaidoPlan is not competing with it.

## What is still missing

A tracker stores tasks. It does not schedule them. There is no project window to violate, no dependency graph to propagate, no slack to compute, and therefore no critical path — which means the one question a delivery date depends on is answered by whoever is most confident in the standup.

Linear / Todoist + MCP

KaidoPlan

Primary job

Capture, assign, track states

Schedule: dependencies, dates, critical path

Dependencies

Blocking links exist; they do not produce a schedule

Propagated forward and backward to produce dates and slack

End date

Set by a human, tracked against

Computed from the graph, and re-computed when the graph changes

Conflict detection

Overdue flags on individual items

Cycles, deadline conflicts, out-of-window tasks, blocked chains

Where it lives

Vendor cloud, per-seat pricing

Local `.kaido` file, $9.99/year for one person

Team features

Strong: comments, roles, notifications

None. It is a single-user planning tool.

## The honest division of labour

Teams that ship on a date tend to use both, in one direction: the plan decides what the dates are, the tracker decides who is told about them. The plan is the arithmetic; the tracker is the notification system. What does not work is maintaining the date in both places by hand — the two copies diverge within a week, and the tracker wins because it is the one people open.

For a solo developer or a two-person project, the tracker's team features are dead weight and the missing schedule is the whole problem. That is the case KaidoPlan is built for: one local file, a dependency graph, a computed end date.

## When the tracker wins

- You need comments, mentions and notifications across a team of five or more.

- The deadline is externally fixed and simply has to be tracked, not derived.

- You work across macOS, Windows and Linux, and a per-seat subscription is fine.

If none of those apply and you are still maintaining dates by hand in a tracker, you are paying a subscription to store a number you cannot verify.

## Questions this page does not answer

Can KaidoPlan sync tasks to Linear or Todoist?

No. There is no two-way sync, and adding one would recreate the divergence problem above. The plan file is plain JSON and the CLI is scriptable, so an export based on a file you own is possible without a sync contract.

Does KaidoPlan work for a team?

It is a single-user tool. The plan file can live in a shared repository, so a small team can read the same plan, but there are no roles, comments or notifications.

KaidoPlan runs on macOS 14 or later.

Try every feature free for 30 days with the direct download. Continue with full access for $9.99 per year.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/compare/kaidoplan-vs-excel-gantt.html

Comparison

# KaidoPlan vs a spreadsheet Gantt

The spreadsheet was never the problem. The problem is that an agent cannot safely be the one editing it.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## What a spreadsheet genuinely does well

A sheet with a date column and conditional formatting is a real Gantt for small projects. It is free, everyone can open it, the formulas are yours, and a project manager who knows the file can predict exactly how it behaves. Nothing below argues that this is unprofessional.

Three things it does badly matter more than they used to:

- A formula is not a scheduler. A sheet can subtract dates. Turning dependencies into earliest and latest start dates, propagating them through a chain, and computing slack is a graph algorithm that most sheets only approximate — usually by having a human look at it.

- There is no schema. A moved column, a merged cell, or a date typed as text breaks the logic silently. The sheet does not fail; it reports a wrong date with full confidence.

- An agent cannot safely write to it. This is the decisive one. The plan is now edited by Claude Code, Codex or a similar agent, and a spreadsheet is the worst possible target for programmatic edits: no schema, no validation, and a single misplaced row silently corrupts the schedule.

## Side by side

Spreadsheet Gantt

KaidoPlan

Scheduling

Formulas you maintain

Forward/backward propagation, critical path, per-task slack

Validation

Whatever you built, if anything

Cycles, deadline conflicts, out-of-window tasks listed as violations

Machine editing

Fragile: cells, formats, merged ranges

Documented JSON with `formatVersion`, 21 MCP tools, CLI

Diff in review

Binary-ish, noisy

Text JSON, one line per change

Platform

Anywhere

macOS 14 or later

Cost

Free to a subscription

$9.99/year after a 30-day free trial via direct download

## When the spreadsheet wins

If the plan is edited by people only, on mixed operating systems, and someone enjoys maintaining the formulas, the sheet is fine — and moving it would cost more than it returns. The case for KaidoPlan begins the moment an agent writes to the plan, because then "cannot be silently corrupted" stops being a preference and becomes a requirement.

Migration is not a project: export the task list, import it with `wbs_import`, add the dependencies, and let the schedule compute. The interesting output is not the chart. It is the list of date conflicts your sheet was already hiding.

## Questions this page does not answer

Can I export back to CSV or a spreadsheet?

The plan is a plain JSON file, so any spreadsheet can be fed from it with a short script. The workbench can also export a delivery report.

Does it print a Gantt chart?

The app draws a Gantt in the workbench. It is not a replacement for a slide deck, and it does not try to be.

KaidoPlan runs on macOS 14 or later.

Try every feature free for 30 days with the direct download. Continue with full access for $9.99 per year.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/qa/sync-plan-across-claude-code-sessions.html

Answer

# How do I keep a project plan in sync across Claude Code sessions?

Short answer: stop keeping the plan in the conversation. Put it in a file, give the agent a documented way to read and write it, and recompute the schedule after every write.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## Why sessions drift

Each Claude Code session starts with whatever context it was given and ends with a transcript. A plan that lives inside that transcript is lost or partially summarised at the boundary, so the next session rebuilds it from prose — and rebuilds it slightly differently. Two sessions later, two versions of the plan exist and neither is authoritative.

The fix is not a better summary. It is separating the plan from the conversation:

- A file owns the plan. Not a chat, not a scratchpad. One file in the repository, with a schema, that outlives every session.

- The agent reads it at the start of a session. One tool call or one `cat`, not a hand-written recap.

- The agent writes to it explicitly. Status, actual dates and new tasks go through defined operations rather than a paragraph asking a human to update a spreadsheet.

- Dates get recomputed after the write. The reason to do 1–3 at all: a write that changes a date can create a conflict, and only a recomputation will say so.

## What this looks like with KaidoPlan

The plan is a single `.kaido` file — plain JSON, `formatVersion` 2 — so a session can read it with nothing installed. With the app running, an MCP server exposes 21 tools over the same file: `task_list` and `project_summary` to read, `status_update` and `status_batch_update` to write back, `schedule_compute` and `violations_list` to check the arithmetic afterwards. The CLI covers the same ground when the app is closed.

`# start of session
kaidoplan project summary --file plan.kaido
# after the agent reports progress
kaidoplan status batch --file plan.kaido --json
kaidoplan violations --file plan.kaido`

Because the file is in the repository, the plan's history is the commit history. A date that moved is a diff you can review, not a claim you have to take on trust.

## The parts that are easy to get wrong

- Letting the agent invent dates. An agent that both plans and executes will optimistically compress durations. Keep the estimates human-owned.

- Skipping the recompute. A status write without a schedule recompute is how a plan accumulates silent contradictions.

- Keeping a second copy in the handoff file. Two sources of dates diverge; the file that gets opened more wins.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does it work without the app running?

Yes for reading and writing the file with the CLI, and for any tool that can parse JSON. The MCP server is the app's own surface and needs the app running.

Can several sessions use the plan at once?

Sequentially, yes — each write lands in the file. Concurrent writers are not coordinated, so treat the plan like a code file being edited: one session at a time.

KaidoPlan runs on macOS 14 or later.

Try every feature free for 30 days with the direct download. Continue with full access for $9.99 per year.

Download KaidoPlanPricing

-

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/qa/ai-agent-marked-everything-done.html

Answer

# The agent marked every task done — why did the deadline still slip?

Because done is a property of a task, and the delivery date is a property of a graph. Nobody was lying; the two never had to agree.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## Three ways a finished list produces a late project

### 1. A task finished after the thing that depended on it started

Agents execute in the order they are asked, which is not always the order the plan implies. Server work finishes on the 6th, client integration began on the 4th, and both statements are true. Nothing in a task list objects, because a task list does not know that one had to precede the other. A schedule does: it reports the pair as a date conflict.

### 2. The dependency was never written down

Most plans record tasks and dates and stop there. Without an edge between two tasks, the schema has no way to say "the acceptance test cannot start before the API exists" — so the schedule compresses, the finish date looks earlier than reality, and the project appears healthy right up to the week it becomes obvious.

### 3. The work that slipped is not on the visible path

Fifteen tasks are green. The two-day delay is in a task nobody watches because it looks small. It is on the critical path, so it moves the end date one-for-one. Everyone optimises what is visible; the date is set by what is on the zero-slack chain.

## The check that catches all three

`kaidoplan schedule compute --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan schedule path --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan violations --file plan.kaido`

Computation gives real dates from the graph. The critical path names the chain that decides the end date. Violations list the conflicts, cycles and out-of-window tasks that a status report cannot see. Run them after every write-back and the three failures above stop being surprises.

## What to change in the process

- Make "done" mean "done, and the plan recomputed".

- Have the agent write status through the tool surface instead of telling you about it — `status_update` records the completion time, which is what a conflict check needs.

- Keep a baseline before each delivery push, so "slipped" is measurable against a frozen schedule rather than a memory.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does the app edit the plan automatically?

Only when an agent or you call a write tool, and only with a Pro licence after the trial. Nothing is rewritten behind your back.

Can I see which task caused the slip?

Yes — the critical path plus the violation entry identifies the tasks with zero slack and the pair whose dates disagree. That is the audit trail, and it is why the plan is kept as a file.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/qa/critical-path-for-ai-projects.html

Answer

# What is a critical path, and why does an AI project need one?

The critical path is the longest chain of dependent work in the plan. Its length is the project's duration, and every task on it has zero slack — delay one by a day and the delivery date moves by a day.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The definition, without the mystique

Take the dependency graph. For every task, compute the earliest it can start and finish, then the latest it can start and finish without pushing the project end. The difference between the two is slack. Tasks with zero slack sit on the critical path, and they form one or more chains from the start of the project to its end.

Two consequences follow, and they are the whole practical value:

- The end date is not the sum of all estimates. It is the length of one chain. Adding people to tasks off the chain buys you nothing.

- Any date change on the chain moves the delivery date one-for-one. That is the only set of tasks where "we lost a day" is literally true.

## Why AI-assisted projects need it more, not less

An agent executes quickly and reports honestly, so the plan fills with completed work — and the natural conclusion is that the project is going well. But agents also compress durations when asked to estimate, and they execute in the order requested rather than the order the graph requires. Both inflate the apparent progress while the chain that sets the date is unchanged.

A checklist cannot see this, because the checklist has no edges. The number that matters is not "how many tasks are done" but "how many days of zero-slack work remain".

## Computing it

`kaidoplan schedule path --file plan.kaido`

Returns the tasks whose total slack is within the requested limit, together with the schedule. In the app the same chain is highlighted in the Gantt chart. Both read the same dependency graph, so they cannot disagree.

## Three practical rules

- Review the critical path, not the task list. If a standup asks everyone for status, it optimises the wrong set. Ask what moved on the chain.

- Keep the chain short on purpose. Parallelising off-chain work is cheap; serialising on-chain work is what makes a plan fragile.

- Recompute after every change. The critical path moves. A chain that was slack last week can become the constraint this week, silently.

## Questions this page does not answer

Do I need to understand the algorithm to use it?

No. You need to trust the graph, which means every dependency you assert has to be real. A wrong edge produces a confidently wrong critical path.

What is the difference between the critical path and the finish date?

The finish date is the output. The critical path is the explanation: which tasks, in which order, produce that date.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/qa/critical-path-on-mac.html

Answer

# How do I calculate a critical path on a Mac?

Use a tool that reads the dependency graph and recomputes the chain whenever a date changes. On macOS that means three options: a planner built around dependencies, a general project management app, or a spreadsheet. Only the first one keeps the answer correct after the third edit.

Updated 2026-11-17 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The three options on macOS

- A planner that computes the chain itself. You enter tasks, durations and dependencies; the tool runs a forward and backward pass and highlights the zero-slack chain. The answer updates when any input changes.

- A general project management app. Many of them compute a critical path. They are built around team collaboration and boards, so the dependency editor is usually a secondary screen and the schedule is derived from assignments rather than from the graph.

- A spreadsheet. Free, and correct for a plan with a handful of tasks and a single chain. It stops being correct as soon as the graph branches, because you have to describe the calculation in formulas and keep them in a valid order.

There is no macOS-specific algorithm here. The calculation is the same on every platform. What differs on a Mac is where the plan lives and who can read it, which matters more than it sounds when AI agents are part of the work.

## Doing it by hand, and where it breaks

The manual version is two passes over the graph:

- Forward pass. For each task in dependency order, earliest start is the latest earliest finish among its predecessors; earliest finish is earliest start plus duration.

- Backward pass. From the project end backwards, latest finish is the earliest latest start among its successors; latest start is latest finish minus duration.

- Slack. Latest start minus earliest start. Zero means the task is on the critical path.

This is correct and it is also where most hand calculations go wrong, in three specific ways:

- Order matters and is invisible in a spreadsheet. A row that reads a value not yet recalculated returns a stale number, quietly. The error shows up as a plausible plan, not as an error.

- A task with two successors needs the minimum, not the first one you look at. Missing the second successor makes a critical task look slack.

- Constraints are not part of the textbook algorithm. A fixed delivery date, a task that cannot start before a date, or a calendar with non-working days has to be folded in, and a spreadsheet has no place to put it.

## Running it locally on a Mac

KaidoPlan is a macOS app that keeps the WBS, the dependency edges and the dates in one local `.kaido` file — plain JSON, no database, no account. The schedule engine computes the critical path, total and free slack, and reports violations: date conflicts, dependency cycles and tasks scheduled outside their allowed window.

The same calculation is available without opening a window:

`kaidoplan schedule path --file plan.kaido`

The CLI and the MCP server are the same engine the app uses, so a command-line answer and the highlighted chain in the Gantt chart cannot disagree. Both are read-only without a licence; writing task status, actual dates or new tasks back into the plan needs Pro.

## Why "on a Mac" changes the answer

For a local-first tool the platform question is mostly a data question. Three consequences that do not apply to a web planner:

- The file is yours. A `.kaido` plan can be diffed, reviewed in a pull request, or kept next to the code it describes. There is no export step and no vendor copy of the schedule.

- Agents read the same file. Claude Code, Codex and other MCP clients read the plan through stdio; the plan does not have to be synchronised into a service first.

- No connection, no account. The 30-day trial requires neither. When it ends the app drops to the free tier — the whole planning workbench, AI read-only, and three delivery-report exports a month — it does not stop.

The trade-off is stated plainly on the product page: this is a single-user local tool. There is no real-time multi-user editing, no cloud sync, and no Windows or Linux build. Sharing a plan with another person means sending the file.

## Questions this page does not answer

Can I calculate a critical path in a spreadsheet on a Mac?

Yes, for a small plan and with care. You do a forward pass for earliest start and finish, a backward pass for latest start and finish, then subtract. It breaks down once a task has more than one successor, or when a calendar or a fixed deadline enters the model, because a spreadsheet recalculates rows in an order you did not choose.

Does the calculation need a cloud account on macOS?

Not with KaidoPlan. The plan is one local .kaido JSON file and the schedule is computed in the app on the machine. There is no account and nothing is uploaded, so the file can live in a git repository or iCloud Drive without sending the plan to a third party.

Can an AI agent read the critical path on a Mac?

Yes, read-only and without a licence. The CLI and the MCP server expose 21 tools over stdio JSON-RPC, and reading plans is free. Writing task status, actual dates or new tasks back into the plan needs a Pro licence.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/qa/wbs-for-ai-coding-projects.html

Answer

# How do I break an AI coding project into a WBS?

Break it down by what can be verified independently, not by what feels like a phase. The test of a good task is that someone can say whether it is done without reading the code.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The unit of breakdown: verification, not activity

Most WBS advice divides projects by activity — design, build, test, ship. That is a reporting structure, not a work structure. For a project executed by an agent, the useful unit is the smallest piece of work whose completion can be checked by a fact rather than an opinion: a route that responds, a migration that applies, a report that totals correctly.

Three rules follow:

- If you cannot describe the check, the task is not small enough. "Improve the importer" has no check; "import a 1PUX export with attachments and reconcile the item count" does.

- Separate planning from execution in the structure. The estimate is a human judgement; making the agent produce both the task and its duration is how plans become optimistic.

- Model groups and milestones, not just tasks. Groups carry the hierarchy reviewers need; milestones are the points where someone other than the author has to agree.

## A shape that works

- Acceptance criteria first. What has to be true on the delivery date, in observable terms.

- Chains that end at a milestone. Group tasks so each group produces one verifiable milestone, then connect the milestones.

- Integration and review as their own tasks. They are the ones that get eaten when the plan is compressed, and they are the ones whose loss shows up as a late project.

- Effort estimates in hours or days, per task. Coarse is fine; absent is not, because without estimates there is no schedule to compute.

## Getting it into the tool

If the breakdown already exists as a nested outline, import it rather than retyping: `wbs_import` turns a nested task tree into the plan. Then add the dependencies — that step is where the real design work happens, because a WBS without edges cannot produce a critical path.

`kaidoplan wbs import --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan schedule compute --file plan.kaido`

## The failure to avoid

An agent generates sixty tasks in a flat list with no dependencies and no estimates. It looks like thorough planning and it is unusable: nothing can be scheduled, nothing can be checked, and the only thing it supports is the illusion that the project is understood.

## Questions this page does not answer

How many tasks is too many?

When you stop being able to name the critical path. For a solo project a few dozen is usually the ceiling; beyond that, groups should hide detail.

Should the agent write the WBS?

It can draft one quickly, and that is useful. Review the edges and the estimates before you schedule anything — those two are where the optimism lives.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/qa/track-dependencies-between-ai-tasks.html

Answer

# How do I track dependencies between tasks an agent executes?

Record them as data, not as instructions in a prompt. A dependency in a chat message is a suggestion; a dependency in the plan is an edge the scheduler will enforce.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## Two kinds of dependency, one place to keep them

Hard dependencies are structural: the acceptance test cannot run before the endpoint exists. Constraints are calendar facts: the security review cannot start before the 12th because the reviewer is away. Both affect the schedule, and both belong in the plan.

Kind

Example

What it changes

Finish-to-start

Client integration starts when the server task ends

Propagates dates; creates the chain

Lag

Two days of review after the build

Adds duration to the edge rather than the task

Start no earlier than

A review that cannot begin before a date

Delays the task; can push the end date

Finish no later than

A demo that cannot slip

Creates a deadline conflict when violated

## Why prompts are the wrong storage

Telling an agent "do the API first, then the client" works for one session. It does not survive the session, it cannot be checked, and it silently disappears when the conversation is summarised. A dependency stored in the plan survives everything, and — the part that matters — the scheduler can prove that the resulting dates are consistent with it.

`kaidoplan task update --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan schedule compute --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan violations --file plan.kaido`

After the edges are in, a cycle is reported rather than discovered later, and a task scheduled before its predecessor ends is a violation instead of a surprise.

## Practical discipline

- One edge, one reason. If you cannot state why the dependency exists, delete it. Invented edges make the critical path fiction.

- Do not model "related to". Undirected relations are not dependencies and add noise to the schedule.

- Re-check after parallelisation. Splitting work changes the graph; the critical path you knew last week may no longer be the constraint.

- Keep the graph in the repository. The plan is a file, so the dependency structure is reviewable in a diff — which is the only way a second person can audit it.

## Questions this page does not answer

Can an agent add dependencies itself?

Yes, through the write tools, on a Pro licence after the trial. Whether it should is a policy question: edges change the delivery date, so many teams keep them human-owned.

What happens if I create a loop?

The schedule cannot be computed, and the cycle is reported as a violation. That is the correct failure: a loop means a piece of work can never start.

Answer

# Is there an MCP server for a project plan?

Yes — KaidoPlan has one built in. 21 tools over stdio or a loopback HTTP endpoint, covering tasks, dependencies, resources, baselines, scheduling and violation checks.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## What the server exposes

The plan is a local file; the MCP server is a second surface on the same data, so an agent can ask questions and make changes without parsing JSON by hand.

Group

Tools

What it is for

Project

`project_create`, `project_open`, `project_save`

Open the plan, create one, save it back to disk

Tasks and WBS

`task_add`, `task_list`, `task_get`, `task_update`, `task_delete`, `wbs_import`

Read and change the structure

Scheduling

`schedule_compute`, `schedule_critical_path`

Turn dependencies into dates and slack

Violations

`violations_list`

Cycles, deadline conflicts, out-of-window tasks

Write-back

`status_update`, `status_batch_update`

Record progress and completion times

Resources

`resource_add`, `resource_list`

People, equipment, materials

Baselines

`baseline_create`, `baseline_list`, `baseline_delete`, `baseline_variance`, `baseline_set_color`

Freeze a schedule, then compare plan and actuals

Twenty-one tools in total. Client setup is one switch per client — Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and WorkBuddy — and the switch writes only the `mcpServers.kaidoplan` key, leaving the rest of the configuration untouched.

## The security model, in three lines

- Loopback only: the endpoint listens on `127.0.0.1`, never the LAN or the internet.

- Every request carries a token the app generates locally and shows in its panel.

- Only folders you authorized in that panel are reachable; anything else is refused.

## Read versus write

The free trial lets an agent read the plan and update task status, actual dates and tasks. Continued use of write-back requires a subscription. Review updates that could move the delivery date.

If you would rather not add an MCP client, the CLI exposes the same operations from a shell, and the file itself is readable JSON.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does it work with a remote or hosted agent?

No. The endpoint is loopback-only by design, so the agent has to run on the same Mac.

Is the server on by default?

Yes since v3.4.0, on 127.0.0.1 with a token. Turning it off in the panel stops access immediately; a previous explicit off setting is not overridden by the default change.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/qa/why-ai-projects-miss-deadlines.html

Answer

# Why do AI-assisted projects still miss deadlines?

Because writing code faster does not shorten the chain that decides the end date — and it makes the plan look healthy while that chain stays exactly as long as it was.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## 1. The estimate was the agent's

An agent asked how long a task will take answers with an average case and no memory of the last time this class of task went wrong. Multiply that optimism across forty tasks and the plan is short before any work starts. Speed does not fix an estimate, it just makes the resulting slip more surprising.

## 2. Dependencies lived in prompts

If the order was communicated in a message instead of recorded in a graph, nothing enforces it. Work starts early, finishes after the thing that needed it, and every individual status is true.

## 3. Integration was treated as a task at the end

Integration, review and acceptance are where compression goes to hide. They are also the tasks most likely to be estimated at zero because they feel like a formality. A plan without them looks a week shorter and is a week wrong.

## 4. The wrong tasks were being watched

A daily report over forty green tasks trains everyone to look at volume. The delivery date is set by the zero-slack chain, which is usually two or three tasks and rarely the ones discussed in standup. Optimising the visible set feels productive and moves nothing.

## What actually helps

- Human-owned estimates, agent-owned execution. The agent writes code; the person who has shipped before sets the duration.

- A dependency graph with real edges, so the schedule can be computed rather than asserted.

- The four checks after every change: compute, critical path, violations, and confirmation that write-back landed.

- Baselines, so "we slipped" is measured against a frozen schedule rather than a remembered one.

None of this makes the project faster. It makes the slip visible on the day it happens instead of the week it becomes undeniable — which is the only window in which a deadline can still be protected.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does the tool shorten the critical path?

No. It tells you which chain sets the date so you can decide what to cut or parallelise. The decision stays yours.

Is this a scheduling problem or a communication problem?

Both, but the scheduling error is the one that cannot be argued with. That is why it is worth computing first.

Answer

# How do I export a delivery report for a client?

A delivery report is not a screenshot of a task list. It answers three questions in order: what is the date, what decides it, and what changed since the last report.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## What belongs in the report

- The computed finish date, not the date someone hoped for.

- The critical path — the chain that produces that date, named by task.

- Violations, including ones that are still open. A report that hides an open conflict is a report that will be contradicted next week.

- Variance against a baseline: planned versus actual per milestone, so "on track" is a measurement.

## Exporting

Preview and export delivery reports from the workbench. You can export as many reports as you need during the trial and with an active subscription. Use the preview to verify the numbers before you send a report.

If you want the same content without a document, the numbers come from the CLI:

`kaidoplan schedule compute --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan schedule path --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan violations --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan baseline variance --file plan.kaido`

## The habit that makes reports cheap

Take a baseline at the start of each reporting period. Then the report is a comparison — plan against actual — instead of a narrative written from memory. It also removes the most common argument in a delivery review: whether the date "changed" or was always wrong.

Keep the plan in the repository and the report has a source you can point at. That is a stronger position than a slide deck nobody can audit.

## Questions this page does not answer

Can I export to PDF or CSV?

The app's delivery report export is the supported path. The plan file is plain JSON, so any other format is a short script away if you need one.

Can I export reports during the free trial?

Yes. The trial includes unlimited delivery-report exports.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/project-files.html

Features · 3 tools

# The plan is a file, not an account

Three tools, one object: a `.kaido` file you can copy, diff, back up and read without the app.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The three tools

Tool

Does

`project_create`

Creates a project. Optional `projectStart` / `projectEnd` (ISO 8601) set the window that scheduling and violation checks are measured against.

`project_open`

Opens a `.kaido` file. Reports `formatVersion` and whether a save would upgrade the file.

`project_save`

Saves to the open file, or acts as save-as when a path is given.

## Why the format matters

The plan is plain JSON with a `formatVersion` field, currently 2. That single decision carries most of the properties people actually want:

- It goes in the repository. Next to the code, reviewed in the same pull request, with one-line diffs when a date moves.

- It outlives the tool. If this app disappears tomorrow, the plan is still a JSON document with a documented shape.

- It is inspectable without permission. An agent, a script or a person with `jq` can read it. No export step, no API key.

- It is local. No account, no sync, no server copy. The app's only unprompted network call is the update check.

## What "formatVersion" buys you

When the schema changes, the app knows what it is reading and upgrades on save, reporting `upgradedFrom` once so the change is visible rather than silent. Older files open; newer files are not silently rewritten.

## The project window is not metadata

Setting a start and an end date is what makes a task "outside the project window" detectable. Without a window, the violation checks have nothing to compare against, and the plan degrades into a list with dates attached.

## Questions this page does not answer

Can I edit the file by hand?

It is plain JSON, so yes — and the app will load it. Keep the schema intact; the CLI and MCP tools are the safer path for structural changes.

Is there a sync service?

No. Put the file in whatever repository or backup you already trust.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/tasks-and-wbs.html

Features · 6 tools

# Tasks and the WBS

Six tools that cover the structure: create, read, filter, change, delete, and bulk import a breakdown you already have.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The tools

Tool

Does

`task_add`

Creates a task with effort, assignee, dependencies and constraints. A constraint is written as `type:ISO8601`, e.g. `startNoLaterThan:2026-11-05T00:00:00Z`.

`task_list`

Lists tasks, optionally filtered by parent or by a natural-language filter.

`task_get`

Returns one task in full — the cheap way to check state before changing it.

`task_update`

Changes fields. Passing an empty string to `assignee` clears the owner rather than writing a blank one.

`task_delete`

Deletes a task and its subtasks, and drops dependencies that pointed at them, so no dangling edges are left behind.

`wbs_import`

Bulk-imports a nested task tree instead of retyping a breakdown that already exists.

## Structure, not fields

Groups carry hierarchy; milestones are the points where someone else has to agree; tasks carry the work, an estimate and the edges. An agent that only adds flat tasks produces a list that cannot be scheduled — which is the most common way a "generated plan" fails.

## Importing what you already have

`wbs_import` takes a nested tree and turns it into the plan. The estimate and the dependency step that follow are the ones that need a human: an imported outline with no edges schedules to a single day, and the resulting date is meaningless rather than wrong.

`kaidoplan wbs import --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan task list --file plan.kaido`

## Deletion is honest

A deleted task takes its dependencies with it. The alternative — leaving edges pointing at a task that no longer exists — produces a schedule that either fails or silently ignores the edge, and both outcomes are worse than a clean delete.

## Questions this page does not answer

Do milestones behave like zero-duration tasks?

They are the points that other tasks depend on, which is why they matter for the schedule. Treat them as checkpoints, not as work.

Can an agent rewrite the whole plan at once?

It can call the write tools in sequence. There is no bulk overwrite operation, and that is intentional: a plan replaced wholesale is a plan nobody reviewed.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/scheduling.html

Features · 2 tools

# Scheduling and the critical path

Two tools turn a dependency graph into an answer: when does this finish, and which tasks decide that.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## schedule_compute

Propagates dependencies forward and backward and returns, for every task, its earliest and latest start and finish, plus the schedule that was chosen. Forward propagation answers "when could this happen"; backward propagation answers "when must it happen without moving the end date". The gap between the two is slack, which is the number that tells you where you have room.

Constraints participate: a task with a start-no-earlier-than constraint is delayed even when its predecessor would allow an earlier start, and a finish-no-later-than constraint is what turns into a deadline conflict when the arithmetic cannot satisfy it.

## schedule_critical_path

Returns the tasks whose total slack is within a limit. With the limit at zero you get the chain that sets the finish date — usually two or three tasks, rarely the ones that dominate a status meeting.

`kaidoplan schedule compute --file plan.kaido
kaidoplan schedule path --file plan.kaido`

## Why compute instead of tracking

A tracked date is a claim. A computed date is a consequence of the graph, and it changes when the graph changes — including when it changes for a reason nobody noticed. That is the whole value: the number moves when reality moves, not when someone remembers to update it.

Estimates remain human input. The scheduler does arithmetic on what you assert; it does not know that the last three integrations took four days instead of two.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does it support resources levelling?

Resources carry units and efficiency and take part in effort conversion. Full resource-levelled scheduling is not something to assume; check what the app shows for your plan rather than trusting a page.

Can I schedule backwards from a fixed delivery date?

Yes — backward propagation is what produces latest dates, and a finish-no-later-than constraint anchors the end.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/violations.html

Features · 1 tool

# Violation checks

The plan admits what is broken, on demand, in a list you can act on.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The four classes

Violation

What it means

Dependency cycle

Two or more tasks wait on each other, so the schedule cannot be computed.

Deadline conflict

A task cannot finish by its constraint or the project end date.

Task outside the project window

Scheduled to start before the project starts or end after it ends.

Blocked chain

Work that cannot proceed because an upstream item is not moving.

## Why a list beats a warning icon

A single red indicator tells you something is wrong and nothing else. A list is actionable: each entry names the tasks involved, so the response is a decision rather than an investigation. Break the cycle, move the date, cut the scope, or accept the slip deliberately.

`kaidoplan violations --file plan.kaido`

## In the workbench

The same checks surface in the app, inline with the plan, so a violation is visible while you are editing rather than at the end of a reporting cycle. Same data, same rules — the CLI and the app do not have separate opinions.

## The honest limitation

These are consistency checks, not feasibility checks. A plan with no violations can still be undeliverable because every estimate is optimistic. Violations tell you the arithmetic holds; only history tells you the estimates were real.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does it check for resource over-allocation?

The listed classes are cycle, deadline conflict, out-of-window task and blocked chain. Do not assume more than that without checking your own plan.

Should violations block a commit?

They can, if you run the CLI in CI. Whether to block is a policy decision — a cycle almost always should.

KaidoPlan runs on macOS 14 or later.

## https://kaidoplan.cygnusyang.top/features/status-writeback.html

Features · 2 tools

# Status write-back

The difference between an agent that reports progress and one that records it: a completion time that a conflict check can use.

Updated 2026-11-16 · by cygnus, the developer of KaidoPlan

## The tools

Tool

Does

`status_update`

Writes status and progress for one task. Setting a task done records the completion time.

`status_batch_update`

Writes many entries at once and returns per-entry success and failure. A failing entry does not stop the remaining ones.

## Completion time is the point

"Done" as a boolean is enough for a burndown and useless for a schedule. The date a task actually finished is what determines whether the task that depended on it started too early — which is the most common real cause of a slipped date in an agent-driven project.

`kaidoplan status batch --file plan.kaido --json`

## Partial success looks like success

Bulk writes deliberately do not abort on the first failure. That is the right behaviour for a long list, and it means the response has to be read: nine of ten entries landing is a state you want to know about, not a state to infer.

## Write access is a paid feature

You can try AI write-back during the free trial. Continued use of write-back requires a subscription. Review schedule changes after an agent updates tasks that affect the delivery date.

## The loop to run

- The agent writes status through the tools, not through prose.

- The schedule is recomputed.

- Violations are listed.

- Any new conflict gets a decision before the next task starts.

Skip step 2 and the plan accumulates contradictions that only surface when a client asks for a date.

## Questions this page does not answer

Does it save automatically?

Write operations save the session's file when there are unsaved changes, so a client does not have to call a save tool after every update.

Can I reject a write?

You control the tool surface: an agent only has the access you granted. Turning the MCP service off stops writes immediately.
